response:
READING

**The numbers first**

*LINDCASTER budget*
GBP 340,000 ÷ GBP 250 = 1,360 items. Contract conservators can take 70/month and start within 8 weeks of an order. From a late-2026 start, 1,360 items would take roughly 19–20 months, finishing mid-to-late 2028, comfortably inside the 2028-09-30 deadline.

*HAVERSHOLT budget*
GBP 295,000 plant + GBP 45,000 conservation = 180 items. The quote is held to 2027-01-30; ordering on or before that date places the order approximately 17–18 weeks before the 2027-05-29 commissioning, which is comfortably inside the 14-week lead time Threlkeld requires. No timing problem.

*Rate of loss*
The unusable band grew from 640 (2019) to 1,010 (2025): 370 items in six years, or approximately 62/year. Under a current-environment scenario, roughly 62 items per year will permanently exit usable status regardless of what else is done.

**What the conservator's report actually says**

Idris Sankey-Marchmont's written professional opinion is that rehousing and aqueous treatment carried out in the strongroom as it stands will need to be repeated within a decade. This is the crux of the decision. The buffered enclosures are stated to hold microclimate within 3 points for 8–12 years. Those two figures bracket almost exactly the same window. LINDCASTER's 1,360 treatments are therefore not durable investments: they are expensive palliatives whose useful life expires at roughly the same moment the protective packaging does, while the underlying chemistry in the collection continues to be driven by a 62% / ±11-point environment. Spending GBP 340,000 to buy a decade's delay is a legitimate triage if no better option exists, but here a better option does exist.

**The environment argument**

The strongroom runs at 62% RH with an 11-point swing. The target is 45–55% with a swing under 5. That is not a marginal exceedance; the humidity alone is 7 percentage points above the top of the acceptable band. High humidity accelerates both acidic hydrolysis (attacking the cellulose and iron-gall items directly) and biological activity. Fixing the environment stops the deterioration clock for all 4,200 items from the moment the plant is commissioned. LINDCASTER treats 1,360 items but leaves all 4,200—including the treated ones—continuing to degrade environmentally. HAVERSHOLT treats only 180 items but converts the remaining 4,020 from an active-decay situation to a stable one.

**The 2029–30 capital programme**

The board sets the 2029–30 programme in November 2028. There is an unallocated GBP 400,000 line with nothing committed against it. Under HAVERSHOLT, the case to the board in November 2028 would be: "The strongroom environment is now correct. We have a conservator's written report confirming that work done in good conditions is permanent. Here are 2,720 at-risk items not yet treated (the 2,900 minus the 180 done now minus attrition). GBP 400,000 would treat 1,600 of them in conditions where the work will last." That is a strong, evidence-based bid to an unallocated line. Under LINDCASTER, the case in November 2028 would be: "We treated 1,360 items but the conservator says the work needs redoing in a decade; we now need GBP 295,000-plus for plant." That is a harder sell, because it implies the Hesketh-Ravenna funds produced an effect that is already time-limited.

**LINDCASTER's genuine strengths**

It is not a careless option. 1,360 treatments versus 180 is a real difference; 1,360 items gain some protection, and the 640+ already-unusable items cannot wait indefinitely. The 62/year attrition rate is alarming, and the at-risk population is large enough that even impermanent treatment buys real time. If the 2029–30 programme fails to materialise, the plant never gets built and the environment never improves, in which case LINDCASTER's impermanent treatments are still better than nothing for those 1,360 items. The dependency on future board decisions is a genuine risk in HAVERSHOLT.

**Weighing the dependency risk**

However: the 2029–30 line is GBP 400,000 unallocated, larger than the GBP 295,000 plant, with nothing committed against it. The board sets it in November 2028—three months after the Hesketh-Ravenna deadline. By that point, under HAVERSHOLT, the institute will have a commissioned, operating environmental control system, a professional conservator's report, and a clean case for conservation expenditure in a now-stable space. The dependency on the 2029–30 programme exists under both courses (LINDCASTER needs it for the plant; HAVERSHOLT needs it for the bulk of the conservation). HAVERSHOLT simply puts the institution in a stronger position to secure it.

**The irreversibility point**

Items that cross into the unusable band are gone. The conservator's professional judgment is that work done now in current conditions is itself impermanent. Those two facts together mean LINDCASTER trades a large sum of money for results that are partial, temporary, and set against an environment that will continue to push items across the unusable threshold. HAVERSHOLT halts the environmental driver of deterioration for the whole collection and ensures that whatever conservation is done—now or in 2029–30—is not wasted.

**Conclusion**

The decisive asymmetry is durability. LINDCASTER buys a decade's delay at full cost and leaves the underlying problem unsolved. HAVERSHOLT solves the underlying problem, treats a smaller number of items durably, and positions the institution to treat the rest durably in 2029–30. The conservator's written report is not a marginal technical note; it is a direct professional statement that the conservation investment in LINDCASTER will not hold.

---

READING
  The quote from Threlkeld is held to 2027-01-30. Ordering by that date places the order ~17–18 weeks before the 2027-05-29 commissioning, comfortably clearing the 14-week lead-time requirement. No timing conflict in HAVERSHOLT. The rate of deterioration (62 items/year into the unusable band) continues under both courses until plant is running; under HAVERSHOLT this stops in May 2027, roughly nine months from now, at a further loss of ~46 items. Under LINDCASTER it continues indefinitely unless the 2029–30 programme is secured. LINDCASTER treats 1,360 items at GBP 340,000 but the conservator states in writing that this work will need to be repeated within a decade in current conditions; the 8–12 year life of buffered enclosures coincides almost exactly with that window, confirming the treatment is not durable. HAVERSHOLT fixes the environment for all 4,200 items, treats 180 durably, and positions the institute to make a strong bid for the unallocated GBP 400,000 in the 2029–30 capital programme from a stable base in which further conservation will also be durable. The 2029–30 line is larger than the plant cost, has nothing committed against it, and the board sets it three months after the bequest deadline, by which point a completed HAVERSHOLT installation provides compelling evidence. LINDCASTER's dependency on the 2029–30 programme is for plant; HAVERSHOLT's dependency is for conservation—but HAVERSHOLT makes that bid from a position of demonstrated environmental control rather than demonstrated need for a second round of the same expenditure.

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  The conservator's written finding that treatment in the current environment must be repeated within a decade means LINDCASTER's GBP 340,000 buys only a temporary effect, while HAVERSHOLT corrects the root cause, makes the immediate conservation durable, and positions the institute to secure the unallocated 2029–30 capital line for further permanent treatment.
